strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: localized PET/CT finding generation from full 3D multimodal volumes, where PET is clearly less represented than X-ray/CT report-generation work.

The proposed PETAR-11K dataset and PETAR-Bench are potentially valuable contributions, especially because they link lesion-level text, PET/CT volumes, and 3D masks across whole-body scans rather than only organ-specific settings.

The model design is well motivated: mask conditioning and focal crops directly target the small-lesion problem in volumetric PET/CT, and the ablation table supports the importance of focal prompting, CT context, and mask input.

Evaluation covers many baseline categories, including 2D VLMs, 3D VLMs, finetuned baselines, and a mask-aware method. PETAR-4B shows consistent improvements across lexical, semantic, and clinical-style metrics, including GREEN and RaTEScore.

The manuscript includes a small human-evaluation component and reports correlations between automated metrics and physician scores, which is helpful given the known limitations of n-gram report metrics.
weaknesses: The largest concern is dataset validity. Lesion masks are generated by a heuristic using reported SUVmax and slice number, and lesion descriptions are further reformatted by an LLM, but the paper does not provide sufficient validation of mask accuracy, text extraction accuracy, failure rates, or manual quality control. Since both training and benchmark labels depend on this pipeline, unquantified label noise directly affects the main claims.

The evaluation appears to use PETAR-Bench sampled from the same automatically constructed data distribution as training, with limited information about patient-level splitting, temporal leakage, report/template leakage, or whether near-duplicate longitudinal cases occur across splits. This weakens the evidence for generalization.

Human evaluation is too small and underdescribed for the strength of the clinical claims. The second round involves only 16 lesions from 8 patients per expert, and the paper does not clearly report blinding, inter-rater agreement, rating scales, statistical significance, or model-wise physician scores.

The comparisons may not be fully fair or informative. Several baselines are not naturally designed for PET/CT or mask-conditioned 3D inputs, while finetuning and prompting details are mostly deferred to supplementary material. It is therefore hard to separate architectural gains from adaptation effort and dataset-format advantages.

The model depends on an externally supplied ROI/mask at inference time. The paper frames this as part of a future PETAR pipeline, but the current system does not solve lesion detection or segmentation end to end, which limits the practical automated-reporting claim.

Several key reproducibility details are missing or vague in the main paper: exact train/validation/test split sizes, prompt templates, decoding settings, preprocessing normalization, focal crop size, mask embedding implementation, baseline finetuning recipes, and whether code/model/data will be fully released despite the claim of a public dataset.

The reported automated scores are very high for some overlap metrics after finetuning, suggesting the task may be highly templated or close to extracting/rephrasing report snippets. The paper does not analyze hallucinations, clinically dangerous errors, laterality/anatomy mistakes, or performance by lesion size, tracer, organ, and uptake level.

Presentation quality is uneven: the paper contains many typographical errors, formatting issues, and cramped tables. These are not fatal scientifically, but they make some experimental details difficult to parse and reduce confidence in the care of the submission.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underserved problem: localized PET/CT finding generation with explicit lesion masks, where 3D context, small lesions, and long reports make the task meaningfully different from common 2D radiology VLM settings.

The proposed PETAR-11K resource, if valid and releasable, could be useful because it links PET/CT volumes, lesion masks, and lesion-level textual findings at a scale larger than typical PET/CT public datasets.

The model design is plausible at a high level: combining PET, CT, lesion masks, and focal crops is well motivated for small dispersed lesions, and the ablation indicates that localized/focal information materially improves reported metrics.
The paper attempts a broad evaluation with 2D, 3D, mask-aware, and finetuned baselines, multiple automatic metrics, and some physician evaluation rather than relying only on n-gram overlap.
weaknesses: The central dataset construction is insufficiently validated. Lesion masks are generated automatically from SUVmax and slice references via thresholding, but the paper reports no expert mask-quality assessment, failure rate, inter-reader validation, or analysis of cases where SUV/slice matching is ambiguous. Since the training and benchmark labels depend on this pipeline, this is a consequential weakness.

Claims about dataset public availability and reproducibility are not adequately supported. The manuscript calls PETAR-11K the first publicly available multimodal PET/CT dataset, but gives no access procedure, license, de-identification details beyond a brief statement, train/validation/test split, or release commitment sufficient for reproduction.

The experimental protocol is under-specified in ways that could change the conclusions: patient-level split handling is not described, leakage between multiple lesions/exams from the same patient is not ruled out, preprocessing and prompting details for 2D baselines are unclear, and only selected baselines are finetuned while others are not comparably adapted.

The architecture and training description omit important technical details. Stage 2 has no clear loss/objective; the mask embedding alignment procedure is vague; dimensional compatibility between global and focal tokens is not fully specified; and hyperparameters are deferred to unavailable supplementary material. This makes the method difficult to reproduce.

The evidence for clinical quality is weak relative to the claims. The first human study uses only 100 pairs for metric correlation, and the second uses five physicians but only 16 lesions from 8 patients per expert as described. Scoring criteria, blinding, rater agreement, statistical uncertainty, and comparative significance are not reported.

The reported improvements are not always presented carefully. For example, the text describes PETAR improving BLEU over InternVL3 by 29%, but the table values go from 0.137 to 0.531, which is not a 29% relative improvement. Such inconsistencies reduce confidence in the quantitative analysis.

The ablation does not strongly isolate the claimed mask-aware contribution. The focal prompt appears to account for most of the gain, while adding the mask alone changes metrics only marginally; in some rows, adding CT or mask does not consistently improve all metrics. The paper still frames mask-aware modeling as the main driver without enough support.

The benchmark uses findings derived from clinical reports and then LLM-normalized into a schema, but the paper does not analyze whether models are rewarded for reproducing templated/report-style text rather than clinically grounded lesion understanding. There is also no robust error analysis of hallucinations, incorrect localization, missed measurements, or clinically unsafe outputs.

The comparison to prior work is somewhat shallow. Several baselines are listed as PET-incapable or CT-focused, but the paper does not fully explain how they were adapted to PET/CT inputs, masks, or focal regions, making the fairness of the leaderboard difficult to judge.

Presentation quality is below the expected level for a top-tier submission, with multiple typos, incomplete-looking references, vague statements such as “comprehensive evaluation,” and figures/tables that do not provide enough methodological detail. These are not the primary reason for rejection, but they reinforce the reproducibility concerns.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem: localized report/finding generation for whole-body PET/CT. PET is clinically important and substantially less covered than X-ray/CT in medical VLM work, so the task itself is a meaningful contribution to vision-language modeling.

The dataset contribution is strong. PETAR-11K links 11,356 lesion-level descriptions from 5,126 exams with PET/CT volumes and 3D lesion masks, which appears genuinely valuable given the scarcity of grounded PET/CT resources. PETAR-Bench with 1,170 lesions also provides a useful evaluation target.

The model design is sensible for the domain. Combining PET, CT, lesion masks, and a focal 3D crop directly targets the small-lesion problem, and the architecture is described clearly enough at the conceptual level.

The empirical results are consistently favorable. PETAR-4B substantially outperforms the evaluated 2D/3D VLM baselines and fine-tuned 3D baselines across most automatic metrics, with especially large gains in CIDEr, GREEN, and semantic scores.

The paper includes useful ablations and human evaluation. The correlation analysis showing GREEN aligns best with physician judgment is a helpful contribution for future PET/CT report-generation evaluation.
weaknesses: The dataset construction relies on a complex automatic extraction pipeline using rule-based filters, RadGraph, LLM ensembles, SUVmax/slice matching, and iterative thresholding, but the manuscript gives limited validation of mask and text-label correctness. For a dataset-centered contribution, noise rates, failure modes, and expert verification statistics are important and currently underreported.

The ablation evidence is weaker than the prose claims. Table 4 suggests the focal prompt is the dominant contributor, while mask and CT sometimes provide marginal or mixed gains. The text claims consistent/synergistic improvement, but the reported numbers do not fully support that interpretation.

Reproducibility is only partial from the main paper. Important details are deferred to supplementary material, including hyperparameters, prompt variants, human scoring criteria, and presumably split construction. It is also unclear whether patient-level separation was enforced across train/validation/test, which is crucial for repeated PET exams.

Human evaluation is valuable but limited in scale. The first round uses 100 pairs for metric correlation, and the second round uses only 16 lesions from 8 patients per physician sample; no inter-rater agreement or statistical uncertainty is reported. This limits the strength of claims about clinical utility.

The comparison setup needs more clarity. Some baselines are fine-tuned and others are not, 2D models are likely disadvantaged by the volumetric/mask-conditioned task, and details on how 2D inputs/masks were represented are sparse. This makes the magnitude of superiority harder to interpret.

There are presentation and consistency issues that should be corrected. For example, the stated percentage improvements over InternVL3 appear mathematically inconsistent, Table 4 has formatting problems and a blank baseline row, and the manuscript contains several typos. These do not undermine the core idea but reduce polish and trust in the quantitative discussion.

The method depends on externally generated lesion ROIs at deployment, but detection/segmentation is outside the evaluated pipeline. Since clinical use depends on ROI quality, the paper would be stronger with sensitivity analysis to noisy or imperfect masks.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and underexplored problem: lesion-level PET/CT finding generation. The focus on PET, dual-modality volumetric inputs, and localized findings is well motivated and distinct from the better-studied chest X-ray/CT report generation setting.

The proposed PETARSeg-11K dataset is potentially a strong contribution. Pairing 11,356 lesion descriptions with 3D lesion segmentations across 5,126 whole-body PET/CT exams would be useful to the community if actually released with clear licensing and splits.
The model design is sensible for the task: PET/CT fusion, mask conditioning, and especially a focal crop are appropriate responses to the small-lesion problem in whole-body volumes.
The experimental section compares against a broad set of 2D and 3D VLM baselines, includes finetuned baselines, reports multiple automated metrics, and provides ablations plus qualitative examples.

The physician reader study is a meaningful addition. Five nuclear medicine physicians evaluated anatomical accuracy, interpretation correctness, and clinical utility, and the external AutoPET examples give some evidence of generalization beyond the internal cohort.
weaknesses: The dataset construction depends heavily on automatic report parsing and SUV/slice-based lesion localization, but the manuscript gives limited validation of text-mask alignment quality. The cited 98% contour-location accuracy is from a sample and prior pipeline, but the current dataset’s extraction, normalization, lesion-description pairing, and failure cases are not characterized in enough detail.

The train/test split is underspecified. The paper reports a held-out set of 1175 test samples, but does not clearly state whether splitting is by patient, exam, report, or lesion. A lesion-level split could leak patient/report context across train and test and would materially inflate results.

The ablation results do not fully support the authors’ interpretation. The focal prompt appears to drive most of the gain, while mask-only and CT-only variants slightly underperform the baseline on several metrics. The full non-TS model is not consistently better than focal-only, yet the text claims mask input and CT provide crucial improvements.

The task formulation assumes a lesion mask is already available. This is clinically important, but it narrows the contribution: PETAR is not a complete automated reporting system unless paired with a reliable lesion detector/segmenter. The paper acknowledges this limitation, but the main claims sometimes imply broader automated PET reporting utility.

Baseline fairness is imperfect. The 2D baselines receive only three representative slices, which may be a weak proxy for whole-body 3D PET/CT context. Conversely, not all baselines appear to receive equivalent mask/focal-crop information, making it difficult to isolate architectural advantages from input-conditioning advantages.

The human evaluation is useful but partially weakens the clinical claim: numeric measurements are replaced or excluded because the model hallucinates them. Since SUV, size, and slice measurements are central to PET reports, this is a material limitation rather than just a presentation detail.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The supplement lists some hyperparameters, but important details such as exact splits, preprocessing/windowing, mask generation parameters, release URL/licensing, annotation quality statistics, and full prompts for model training/inference are missing or too sparse.

The claimed public dataset contribution is central, but the manuscript does not provide a concrete release mechanism or access details. For medical data, this matters: without a clear release path, one of the paper’s main contributions remains uncertain.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem: localized PET/CT lesion-level report generation, where whole-body 3D context and small lesion grounding are genuinely challenging.

PETARSeg-11K, if actually released with the claimed PET/CT volumes, lesion masks, and aligned descriptions, would be a useful resource because existing public PET/CT datasets generally lack lesion-level free-text grounding.

The manuscript compares against a reasonably broad set of 2D and 3D VLM baselines, including finetuned variants, and reports both conventional captioning metrics and clinically motivated metrics such as GREEN and RaTE.
The inclusion of a blinded physician evaluation with five nuclear medicine physicians is valuable, and the paper makes a reasonable attempt to relate automated metrics to expert judgments.

The focal-prompt idea is well motivated for lesions occupying less than 0.1% of the scan volume, and the ablation suggests that localized high-resolution crops are the main driver of performance gains.
weaknesses: The central mask-aware modeling claim is not strongly supported by the ablation. Adding the mask alone does not improve performance over the M3D-RAD-like baseline, and with focal prompting the mask adds only marginal or inconsistent gains. The focal crop, not mask-aware conditioning, appears to account for most of the improvement.

The dataset construction depends heavily on LLM extraction and heuristic PET thresholding from report-derived SUVmax and slice numbers, yet there is little direct validation of the generated text-mask correspondence in this dataset. The cited 98% contour-location accuracy appears inherited from prior work rather than a detailed audit of PETARSeg-11K alignment quality.

The task formulation is clinically incomplete: the model is given the lesion mask at inference time, so it does not solve lesion detection, selection, or full report generation. This is a much easier setting than automated PET reporting, but the framing repeatedly implies broader reporting utility.

The human evaluation has important caveats. Quantitative measurements are removed because the model hallucinates them, although these measurements are clinically important and present in the target reports. The external AutoPET evaluation has only 32 cases and no reference reports, automated metrics, or human-report comparison, limiting claims of out-of-distribution performance.

Several experimental details are inconsistent or underspecified. The main text says all stages are trained for 10 epochs, while the supplement lists 5 epochs. The architecture description mixes equations for shared ViT patch embeddings with a figure describing modality-specific 3D convolutional projectors and an M3D-CLIP backbone. Split strategy by patient, scanner, cancer type, and temporal leakage risk is not clearly described.

The claim that the dataset is publicly available is not substantiated in the manuscript with an access link, license, release protocol, or data governance details. Since the data come from hospital records, reproducibility and actual community usefulness are uncertain.

Baseline fairness is questionable. 2D baselines receive only three representative slices, while the proposed method receives full 3D PET, CT, masks, and focal crops. The paper does not clearly isolate whether improvements come from architecture, input privilege, preprocessing, or task-specific finetuning.

The automatic metrics are weak evidence for clinical correctness, and the paper itself shows only moderate correlation with physician scores. Yet many claims of state-of-the-art clinical utility are based primarily on these metrics.

The manuscript overstates conclusions relative to the evidence. Scores around 3.7-3.9 out of 5 for utility and interpretation imply outputs still require nontrivial physician editing, and 47/116 cases were not preferred to human text, which tempers the claim of clinically useful findings.

Reproducibility is limited: preprocessing, prompts, training stages, data filtering, generation settings, and evaluation implementation details are not sufficient to reproduce the dataset or results from the paper alone.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem: lesion-level PET/CT findings generation. The focus on localized PET reporting is well motivated clinically and technically distinct from standard 2D radiology report generation.

PETARSeg-11K is a strong contribution if released as claimed: 11,356 lesion descriptions from 5,126 exams paired with 3D PET/CT lesion masks would fill a real gap in public PET/CT vision-language resources.
The proposed PETAR-4B architecture is sensible for the task. Mask-aware encoding plus a focal 3D crop directly targets the core difficulty that lesions occupy a tiny fraction of whole-body volumes.

The empirical results are convincing overall. PETAR-4B substantially outperforms finetuned 2D and 3D baselines across lexical, semantic, and clinical metrics, with especially large gains in CIDEr, GREEN, and RaTEScore.
The ablation study is useful and shows that the focal prompt is a major driver of performance, while TotalSegmentator pretraining and the full PET/CT/mask setup provide additional gains.

The human evaluation with five nuclear medicine physicians is a notable strength. Reporting anatomical, interpretation, and utility scores, plus correlation between automated metrics and physician judgments, gives the work more clinical credibility than metrics alone.
The manuscript is generally clear, well structured, and gives enough high-level detail to understand the dataset construction pipeline, model design, baselines, and evaluation protocol.
weaknesses: The dataset construction relies on LLM extraction and an iterative SUV/slice-based segmentation pipeline, but validation details are thin. The paper reports 98% contour-location accuracy on a physician-evaluated sample, but does not specify the sample size, sampling strategy, inter-rater process, or failure modes, which matters because the dataset is itself a main contribution.

The claimed public availability is central, but the manuscript does not provide concrete release details, licensing/access conditions, de-identification checks beyond named tools, or whether all PET/CT volumes, masks, and text will actually be downloadable. This weakens reproducibility and practical impact.

The train/test split is described as 1,175 held-out samples, but it is not sufficiently clear whether splitting is by lesion, exam, patient, or institution. Lesion-level splitting within the same exam or patient could inflate results because nearby lesions and report style may leak across splits.

The evaluation partly sidesteps quantitative hallucination: the human study masks numerics because lesion size/SUV can be derived from masks. However, the qualitative examples explicitly show hallucinated measurements, and quantitative values are clinically important in PET reports. Treating this as outside scope is understandable but leaves a meaningful safety gap.

The external validation is promising but small: only 32 AutoPET cases, without reference reports or automated metrics. This limits conclusions about robustness to different institutions, scanners, tracers, protocols, and contrast-enhanced CT distributions.

Baseline fairness is somewhat uncertain. The 2D baselines receive only three representative slices, while PETAR receives full 3D PET/CT plus mask and focal crop. This is reasonable for motivating 3D modeling, but the comparison does not fully isolate architecture from input-information advantage.

The ablation table shows that mask-only and CT-only additions without focal prompting provide little or sometimes negative benefit relative to the base model. The discussion overstates the independent effect of mask and CT relative to the evidence; the focal crop appears to dominate.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete or mildly inconsistent. The main paper says all stages were trained for 10 epochs, while the supplement lists 5 training epochs for LoRA fine-tuning; full finetuning versus LoRA-only tuning is also not completely clear. Code, preprocessing scripts, prompts, and exact baseline adaptation details would be needed to reproduce the results.

The clinical workflow assumption that physicians will provide lesion masks, or that an upstream detector will provide them reliably, is a substantial dependency. The paper evaluates report generation given masks, not the complete automated reporting pipeline, so the title/claims should be interpreted accordingly.
